=== Tools/DbMigrationRunner/README.md ===
# SolutionOne — DB Migration Runner (SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe)

A small Windows tool that does by hand what the web app does at startup: take a folder of `.sql`
scripts (tables, columns, **stored procedures**, views, data fixes), run them against **one or more
databases you tick**, and record what ran in each database's `dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory`.

Useful when you cannot wait for an app restart, when you are setting up a new client database, or
when the same change has to go into every client database in one go.

```
C:\Project\Tools\DbMigrationRunner\bin\Release\SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe
```

## How to use it

1. **Server and databases** — enter the server (`localhost`, or `103.167.223.202` on the server
   itself), pick Windows or SQL auth, then press *Load list* and **tick every database** the scripts
   should go into. *Test connection* checks each ticked database and shows the SQL Server version.
2. **Script folder** — defaults to `C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\App_Data\DbMigrations`. *Browse...* for
   any other folder (e.g. a folder of exported stored procedures). Scripts always run in **filename
   order**, which is why the migration files are numbered.
3. The grid lists every `.sql` file and whether the ticked databases already have it
   (`In history` = Yes / No / *Yes (file changed)* for one database; `3 / 5` for several).
   Untick anything you do not want. Double-click a row to read the script.
4. **▶ Run on N databases** — the prompt lists every database it is about to touch, then the run
   walks through them **one database at a time** and the log shows a `--- [DbName] ---` header for
   each. The grid totals up as it goes (`4 OK, 1 failed`), and the finish dialog lists the result per
   database.
5. **View history table** — reads `HR_SchemaMigrationHistory` and `HR_SchemaMigrationLog` back out of
   the database highlighted in the list, and shows **the last query that was executed** for the
   selected row.

Server, ticked databases, the known database list, login name and folder are remembered between runs
in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolutionOneDbMigrator\settings.txt`. **The password is never saved.**

### Selecting the databases

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Load list** | Reads the user databases off the server. Anything already ticked stays ticked, even if this server does not have it. |
| **Tick all / Tick none** | Applies to what the list currently shows — so filter first, then *Tick all*, to select a group. |
| **Filter** | Narrows the list as you type (e.g. `HR_` to see only the client databases). Ticks are kept while filtering. |
| **Add** | Type a database that is not in the server list and press *Add* or Enter. Several at once: separate with `,` or `;`. |

Each database gets its **own** connection, its own `HR_SchemaMigrationHistory` check and its own
transaction per script, so *Skip scripts already in history* is decided per database — a script
already applied to `HR_A` is still applied to `HR_B`.

With **Stop on first error** ticked, a failure stops that database *and* skips the databases after
it. Untick it to push through every database and get the full list of failures at the end. **Stop**
lets the running script finish, then abandons the rest of the run — databases that have not started
are left untouched.

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Skip scripts already in history** | On (recommended). Off = re-runs the script and refreshes its history row. Judged separately for every ticked database. |
| **Stop on first error** | On = stop at the first failure, and do not start the remaining databases. Off = keep going and report all failures. |
| **Transaction per script** | On = a failing script rolls back completely. Turn off only for statements SQL Server refuses to run inside a transaction (e.g. `ALTER DATABASE`, full-text). |
| **Ignore USE \[database\] lines** | Off by default: a `USE [x]` line is an **error**, because it would silently move the script to another database. Tick it for SSMS-exported proc scripts — the lines are stripped and the removal is logged. |
| **Save full script text in history** | Stores the whole script in `ScriptText` as well as the last batch. |
| **Command timeout** | Seconds per batch. Raise it for long data fixes. |

## What gets written to the database

Both tables live **inside each target database** and are created / extended automatically on
connect, so the tool works against a database that has never seen it. Everything is idempotent.

**`dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory`** — one row per **applied** script, the same table the web app's
`App_Code\DatabaseMigrationRunner.cs` uses, so a script applied by either one is treated as applied
by the other. Original columns (`MigrationID`, `ScriptName`, `AppliedOn`, `AppliedBy`, `Checksum`)
plus, added by this tool:

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Status` | `Success` |
| `DurationMs` | How long the script took |
| `BatchCount` | Number of `GO`-separated batches executed |
| `LastExecutedQuery` | **The last query that ran for this script** |
| `ScriptText` | The full script as executed (optional) |
| `AppliedSource` | `DbMigratorExe` — as opposed to a row written by the web app |

**`dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationLog`** — one row per **attempt**, successes *and* failures, with
`ErrorMessage` and the batch that failed in `LastExecutedQuery`.

Failures are deliberately kept out of the history table: its primary key is `MigrationID`, so a
failure row there would block the retry of that same script. History = "this database has it";
log = "here is everything that was ever tried".

`App_Data\DbMigrations\072_ExtendSchemaMigrationHistory.sql` adds the same columns and table through
the app's own migration runner, so every client database ends up with them either way.

## Getting it onto the server (it publishes with the site)

`build.ps1` copies the built exe into **`C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\RunScripts\`**, which is part of
the web site, so publishing the site carries the tool along:

```
C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\RunScripts\   ->   C:\Publish\RunScripts\   ->   server
```

On the server, double-click `C:\Publish\RunScripts\SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe`. **The folder box fills
itself in**: the tool looks for `..\App_Data\DbMigrations` next to the exe, which resolves to the
site's own deployed migration scripts. Press *Load list*, tick the databases and press Run.

`RunScripts\web.config` blocks HTTP access to the folder (`authorization/deny` plus a hidden
segment), so the exe cannot be downloaded from the live site — it is an admin tool with database
access, and without that file `http://<site>/RunScripts/SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe` would serve it.
Do not delete it.

## Building

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Project\Tools\DbMigrationRunner\build.ps1
```

Uses Visual Studio's MSBuild when present, otherwise the Roslyn `csc.exe` inside
`C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\Bin\roslyn`. Output: `bin\Release\SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe` — a single
.NET Framework 4.8 exe, no dependencies to copy. `DbMigrationRunner.csproj` also opens directly in
Visual Studio 2022.

## Script rules (same as the web app's runner)

- No `USE [database]` — the tool connects to the database you selected.
- Keep everything **SQL Server 2014** compatible; production runs 2014.
- Separate batches with `GO` (required around `CREATE PROCEDURE` / `CREATE VIEW`).
- Make each script **idempotent** (`IF OBJECT_ID(...) IS NULL`, `IF COL_LENGTH(...) IS NULL`, a
  `WHERE` guard on data updates) so re-running is a no-op.
- Keep each script safe to run inside one transaction.

=== Database/README.md ===
# HR Payroll — database scripts

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `FullSchema.sql` | Full baseline schema for **new** database setup |
| `HR_Updates.sql` | **Single consolidated update script** — all incremental changes (001–016). Safe to re-run. |
| `Run-HR-Updates.ps1` | PowerShell wrapper to execute `HR_Updates.sql` via sqlcmd |
| `ClientRegistry.sql` | Creates the master `HR_ClientRegistry` table for single-codebase multi-client deployment |

## New database

1. Restore or execute `FullSchema.sql` on an empty database.
2. Execute `HR_Updates.sql` once to apply all extensions and procedure fixes.

## Existing database

Execute only `HR_Updates.sql` (idempotent — skips objects/columns that already exist).

### SSMS

1. Connect to your server.
2. Open `Database/HR_Updates.sql`.
3. Select the target database.
4. Execute (F5).

### sqlcmd

```cmd
sqlcmd -S YOUR_SERVER -d YOUR_DATABASE -E -I -b -i Database\HR_Updates.sql
```

### PowerShell

```powershell
cd D:\git\hr_payroll\Database
.\Run-HR-Updates.ps1 -Server "SHIVAM" -Database "CryoGas_HR_TestServer" -UseIntegratedSecurity
```

## Multi-client / single-codebase deployment

For long-term deployment, keep **one IIS application folder** and map each host name to a client database:

```text
client1.yourdomain.com -> HR_Client1
client2.yourdomain.com -> HR_Client2
```

Setup:

1. Create a master registry database, for example `HR_Master`.
2. Run `Database/ClientRegistry.sql` in that master database.
3. Insert one row per client into `dbo.HR_ClientRegistry`.
4. Configure `SolutionOneWeb/Web.config`:
   - `EnableMultiTenant=true`
   - `masterConnectionString` points to `HR_Master`
   - `clientConnectionTemplate` points to the SQL Server with any sample database; the application replaces only `Initial Catalog`.

## Auto migration system

The application has a migration runner in `SolutionOneWeb/App_Code/DatabaseMigrationRunner.cs`.

Migration files are stored in:

```text
SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations
```

Every client database gets this tracking table automatically:

```sql
dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory
```

The runner executes only pending scripts per database.

Recommended production flow:

1. Add a new numbered script in `SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations`.
2. Publish the application.
3. Run pending migrations from an admin action or temporarily set:

```xml
<add key="AutoRunMigrationsOnStartup" value="true" />
```

Keep startup auto-run disabled by default until scripts are tested.

## Future SQL changes

For the new multi-client system, add each future change as a separate numbered file in:

```text
SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations
```

Example:

```sql
-- #############################################
-- 017_YourFeature.sql
-- #############################################
-- your idempotent SQL here
GO
```

`HR_Updates.sql` is retained for legacy/manual updates. New production updates should go through the migration folder so each client DB records exactly which scripts were applied.

## What HR_Updates.sql includes (through 016)

| # | Topic |
|---|--------|
| 001 | `HR_AttendancePeriodStatus` |
| 002 | `HR_EmployeeShiftAssignment` |
| 003 | `HR_MachinePunchProcessLog` |
| 004 | `HR_LeavePolicyRule` |
| 005 | Daily attendance processing columns |
| 006 | Attend policy minute columns |
| 007 | `csp_HR_ValidateLeaveApplication` |
| 008 | `HR_UserMaster.UiTheme` |
| 009 | Salary formula builder |
| 010 | `HR_UserUnitRights` |
| 011 | `HR_UserCompanyEmployee` |
| 012 | `HR_CloneMasterLog` |
| 013 | `HR_EditLock` |
| 014 | `HR_UserActiveSession` |
| 015 | Notifications company scope |
| 016 | `HR_GenerateAttendance` INSERT fix |
| 019 | `HR_UserCategoryRights` |
| 020 | Missing baseline tables from full schema |
| 021 | Missing baseline columns from full schema |

## Verify after run

```sql
SELECT name FROM sys.tables
WHERE name IN (
    'HR_AttendancePeriodStatus', 'HR_EmployeeShiftAssignment',
    'HR_UserCompanyEmployee', 'HR_EditLock', 'HR_UserActiveSession'
);

SELECT name FROM sys.procedures
WHERE name IN ('csp_HR_ValidateLeaveApplication', 'HR_GenerateAttendance');
```

```powershell
cd ..
.\Run-HR-Updates.ps1 -Server "YOUR_SERVER" -Database "YOUR_DATABASE" -UseIntegratedSecurity
```

| **Add** | Type a database that is not in the server list and press *Add* or Enter. Several at once: separate with `,` or `;`. |

Each database gets its **own** connection, its own `HR_SchemaMigrationHistory` check and its own
transaction per script, so *Skip scripts already in history* is decided per database — a script
already applied to `HR_A` is still applied to `HR_B`.

With **Stop on first error** ticked, a failure stops that database *and* skips the databases after
it. Untick it to push through every database and get the full list of failures at the end. **Stop**
lets the running script finish, then abandons the rest of the run — databases that have not started
are left untouched.

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Skip scripts already in history** | On (recommended). Off = re-runs the script and refreshes its history row. Judged separately for every ticked database. |
| **Stop on first error** | On = stop at the first failure, and do not start the remaining databases. Off = keep going and report all failures. |
| **Transaction per script** | On = a failing script rolls back completely. Turn off only for statements SQL Server refuses to run inside a transaction (e.g. `ALTER DATABASE`, full-text). |
| **Ignore USE \[database\] lines** | Off by default: a `USE [x]` line is an **error**, because it would silently move the script to another database. Tick it for SSMS-exported proc scripts — the lines are stripped and the removal is logged. |
| **Save full script text in history** | Stores the whole script in `ScriptText` as well as the last batch. |
| **Command timeout** | Seconds per batch. Raise it for long data fixes. |

## What gets written to the database

Both tables live **inside each target database** and are created / extended automatically on
connect, so the tool works against a database that has never seen it. Everything is idempotent.

**`dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory`** — one row per **applied** script, the same table the web app's
`App_Code\DatabaseMigrationRunner.cs` uses, so a script applied by either one is treated as applied
by the other. Original columns (`MigrationID`, `ScriptName`, `AppliedOn`, `AppliedBy`, `Checksum`)
plus, added by this tool:

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Status` | `Success` |
| `DurationMs` | How long the script took |
| `BatchCount` | Number of `GO`-separated batches executed |
| `LastExecutedQuery` | **The last query that ran for this script** |
| `ScriptText` | The full script as executed (optional) |
| `AppliedSource` | `DbMigratorExe` — as opposed to a row written by the web app |

**`dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationLog`** — one row per **attempt**, successes *and* failures, with
`ErrorMessage` and the batch that failed in `LastExecutedQuery`.

Failures are deliberately kept out of the history table: its primary key is `MigrationID`, so a
failure row there would block the retry of that same script. History = "this database has it";
log = "here is everything that was ever tried".

`App_Data\DbMigrations\072_ExtendSchemaMigrationHistory.sql` adds the same columns and table through
the app's own migration runner, so every client database ends up with them either way.

## Getting it onto the server (it publishes with the site)

`build.ps1` copies the built exe into **`C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\RunScripts\`**, which is part of
the web site, so publishing the site carries the tool along:

```
C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\RunScripts\   ->   C:\Publish\RunScripts\   ->   server
```

On the server, double-click `C:\Publish\RunScripts\SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe`. **The folder box fills
itself in**: the tool looks for `..\App_Data\DbMigrations` next to the exe, which resolves to the
site's own deployed migration scripts. Press *Load list*, tick the databases and press Run.

`RunScripts\web.config` blocks HTTP access to the folder (`authorization/deny` plus a hidden
segment), so the exe cannot be downloaded from the live site — it is an admin tool with database
access, and without that file `http://<site>/RunScripts/SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe` would serve it.
Do not delete it.

## Building

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Project\Tools\DbMigrationRunner\build.ps1
```

Uses Visual Studio's MSBuild when present, otherwise the Roslyn `csc.exe` inside
`C:\Project\SolutionOneWeb\Bin\roslyn`. Output: `bin\Release\SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe` — a single
.NET Framework 4.8 exe, no dependencies to copy. `DbMigrationRunner.csproj` also opens directly in
Visual Studio 2022.

## Script rules (same as the web app's runner)

- No `USE [database]` — the tool connects to the database you selected.
- Keep everything **SQL Server 2014** compatible; production runs 2014.
- Separate batches with `GO` (required around `CREATE PROCEDURE` / `CREATE VIEW`).
- Make each script **idempotent** (`IF OBJECT_ID(...) IS NULL`, `IF COL_LENGTH(...) IS NULL`, a
  `WHERE` guard on data updates) so re-running is a no-op.
- Keep each script safe to run inside one transaction.

=== Database/README.md ===
# HR Payroll — database scripts

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `FullSchema.sql` | Full baseline schema for **new** database setup |
| `HR_Updates.sql` | **Single consolidated update script** — all incremental changes (001–016). Safe to re-run. |
| `Run-HR-Updates.ps1` | PowerShell wrapper to execute `HR_Updates.sql` via sqlcmd |
| `ClientRegistry.sql` | Creates the master `HR_ClientRegistry` table for single-codebase multi-client deployment |

## New database

1. Restore or execute `FullSchema.sql` on an empty database.
2. Execute `HR_Updates.sql` once to apply all extensions and procedure fixes.

## Existing database

Execute only `HR_Updates.sql` (idempotent — skips objects/columns that already exist).

### SSMS

1. Connect to your server.
2. Open `Database/HR_Updates.sql`.
3. Select the target database.
4. Execute (F5).

### sqlcmd

```cmd
sqlcmd -S YOUR_SERVER -d YOUR_DATABASE -E -I -b -i Database\HR_Updates.sql
```

### PowerShell

```powershell
cd D:\git\hr_payroll\Database
.\Run-HR-Updates.ps1 -Server "SHIVAM" -Database "CryoGas_HR_TestServer" -UseIntegratedSecurity
```

## Multi-client / single-codebase deployment

For long-term deployment, keep **one IIS application folder** and map each host name to a client database:

```text
client1.yourdomain.com -> HR_Client1
client2.yourdomain.com -> HR_Client2
```

Setup:

1. Create a master registry database, for example `HR_Master`.
2. Run `Database/ClientRegistry.sql` in that master database.
3. Insert one row per client into `dbo.HR_ClientRegistry`.
4. Configure `SolutionOneWeb/Web.config`:
   - `EnableMultiTenant=true`
   - `masterConnectionString` points to `HR_Master`
   - `clientConnectionTemplate` points to the SQL Server with any sample database; the application replaces only `Initial Catalog`.

## Auto migration system

The application has a migration runner in `SolutionOneWeb/App_Code/DatabaseMigrationRunner.cs`.

Migration files are stored in:

```text
SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations
```

Every client database gets this tracking table automatically:

```sql
dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory
```

The runner executes only pending scripts per database.

Recommended production flow:

1. Add a new numbered script in `SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations`.
2. Publish the application.
3. Run pending migrations from an admin action or temporarily set:

```xml
<add key="AutoRunMigrationsOnStartup" value="true" />
```

Keep startup auto-run disabled by default until scripts are tested.

## Future SQL changes

For the new multi-client system, add each future change as a separate numbered file in:

```text
SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations
```

Example:

```sql
-- #############################################
-- 017_YourFeature.sql
-- #############################################
-- your idempotent SQL here
GO
```

`HR_Updates.sql` is retained for legacy/manual updates. New production updates should go through the migration folder so each client DB records exactly which scripts were applied.

content.text:
Yes, it's possible — and you're closer than you think. But my earlier recommendation was wrong in one important way, and your plan needs one correction.

## The thing that changes everything

**Payroll already built this.** `HRMS_Payroll/Tools/DbMigrationRunner/` is a WinForms tool (`SolutionOneDbMigrator.exe`) that runs a folder of numbered scripts against multiple ticked databases and journals them. There's also `SolutionOneWeb/App_Code/DatabaseMigrationRunner.cs` which does the same at app startup, and **239 numbered migration scripts** in `SolutionOneWeb/App_Data/DbMigrations/` (`000_BaselineCatchup` → `251_LoanDirectPayment`).

That's where `HrSchemaMigrationHistory.cs` and `HrSchemaMigrationLog.cs` in your backend's `Entities/` came from — your scaffold picked up Payroll's journal tables out of the shared database. The mystery from last time is solved.

So: **do not build a second journal.** `MigrationID` is the primary key of `HR_SchemaMigrationHistory` and it's just the filename without extension. If you start your own `001_`, `002_` sequence you will collide with Payroll's on the PK. Their README already states the intended contract: *"a script applied by either one is treated as applied by the other."* You want to join that protocol, not compete with it.

## How entangled you actually are

I extracted every table written by `CREATE TABLE`/`ALTER TABLE`/`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` across both repos' SQL:

| | Tables |
|---|---|
| HRMS writes only | 117 |
| Payroll writes only | 97 |
| **Both write** | **117** |

The shared 117 isn't peripheral — it's the core: `HR_EmployeeMaster`, `HR_UserMaster`, `HR_MenuItems`, `HR_SalaryHeadMaster`, `HR_LeaveApplication`, `HR_DailyAttendance`, `HR_MonthlyAttendance`, `HR_LoanRequests`, `HR_ShiftMaster`, `HR_AttendPolicy`, the whole income-tax set, the whole PMS set.

This isn't two systems with a shared fence. It's one schema with two owners and no contract. That's worth naming plainly, because it sets how much the tool has to do.

## Three hazards to fix before any tooling

**1. `AutoRunMigrationsOnStartup` is `true`** in `HRMS_Payroll/SolutionOneWeb/Web.config:389`. Payroll's own README says *"Keep startup auto-run disabled by default until scripts are tested."* Right now, deploying Payroll silently runs pending migrations against **every active client database** — including `ALTER TABLE` on those 117 shared tables — while your API is live against the same data. Turn this off and make migration an explicit step. This is the single most dangerous thing in either repo.

**2. Duplicate migration number**: `230_EmployeeProbation.sql` and `230_GovernmentComplianceMenuText.sql`. They don't collide on the PK (full filename differs), but ordering between them is alphabetical, and "we're at 230" is now ambiguous.

**3. SQL Server 2014 compatibility.** Payroll's runner README pins it: *"Keep everything SQL Server 2014 compatible; production runs 2014."* Your HRMS scripts are newer-dialect in places. Any script touching a shared table inherits the 2014 floor — no `STRING_AGG`, no `TRIM`, no `OPENJSON` niceties.

## What I'd build: two tools, not one

### Tool A — a journal-compatible runner for your side

You still need your own runner, for a reason that has nothing to do with duplication: theirs is .NET Framework 4.8 WinForms, Windows-only, and you work in WSL. Build `SolutionOne_DbMigrator` as a .NET 8 CLI that is a **second client of the same protocol**:

- Writes to the same `dbo.HR_SchemaMigrationHistory` / `HR_SchemaMigrationLog`.
- Same rules: no `USE [db]`, `GO` batch splitting, transaction per script, idempotent scripts, SHA-256 checksum.
- Sets `AppliedSource = 'HrmsCli'` so you can tell at a glance who applied what.
- **Namespaced IDs**: name your scripts `HRMS_20261023_1430__canteen_meal_booking.sql`. Can never collide with Payroll's `NNN_Name.sql`, sorts into its own space, and stays readable in the history table.

If you use DbUp, give it a custom `IJournal` pointed at their table — don't let it create `SchemaVersions`.

Your 157 existing scripts are already idempotent and guarded, so baselining is cheap: run them with an empty journal and the applied ones no-op. The destructive/investigative ones (`Cleanup_`, `Delete_`, `Truncate_`, `Reset_`, `Check_`, `HelperQuery.sql`) go to an `Adhoc/` folder outside the runner, not into the journal.

### Tool B — the schema contract tool (this is the new thing)

This is what you're actually asking for and it genuinely doesn't exist yet. Four jobs:

**1. An ownership manifest** — one checked-in file, identical in both repos, declaring every table as `hrms` / `payroll` / `shared`. I can generate the first draft from the overlap analysis above; you and the Payroll side correct it once. For `shared`, record *what kind* of access each app has — some of those 117 are "Payroll writes, HRMS reads", which is much safer than true co-writing.

**2. A script linter** (pre-commit + CI). Parses a new migration, extracts the objects it touches, and fails if it alters a table you don't own without an explicit annotation:

```sql
-- SHARED-CHANGE: HR_EmployeeMaster
-- NEIGHBOUR-PR: HRMS_Payroll#47
-- COMPAT: SQL2014
```

No annotation, no merge. That turns your "I will keep making pull requests" from a discipline you have to remember into something the repo refuses to let you skip.

**3. A drift detector.** Snapshot each database's columns/indexes/procs into `docs/schema/snapshots/<env>.json`, diff against the previous snapshot, and attribute every change to a journal row. Anything unattributed was done by hand in SSMS or by the neighbour without a script — which is exactly the class of surprise you're trying to stop. Run it nightly per environment.

**4. A cross-repo impact report.** When Payroll adds `252_SomethingOnEmployeeMaster.sql`, the tool reads their folder, finds the tables it touches, and tells you which of your 344 entity classes, repositories and `Specs/` docs reference them. That report *is* the PR you want to raise — and it catches the silent failure mode where Payroll alters a column and your scaffolded entity goes stale without anyone noticing.

Tool B lives in your repo and reads Payroll's repo read-only (sibling checkout or git submodule). It never needs their cooperation to be useful to you — which matters, because it means you can ship it unilaterally.

## One honest caution on the plan

"I will keep both systems updated and keep making pull requests" makes you a single point of failure across two codebases and ~15 contributors. It's fine as the starting state, but build Tool B so the *rules* are enforced by CI rather than by you remembering. The goal is that a Payroll dev who's never heard of your repo still can't merge a change to `HR_EmployeeMaster` without the annotation that triggers your impact report.

The ideal end state is that the 117 shared tables get an owner each and most co-writing becomes one-writer-many-readers. That's a longer conversation with the Payroll side, but the manifest from Tool B is what makes it a concrete negotiation instead of an argument.

## Suggested order

| Phase | Work |
|---|---|
| 0 | Turn off `AutoRunMigrationsOnStartup`; fix the dup `230`; gitignore `appsettings.*.json` and pull the commented connection strings out |
| 1 | Ownership manifest, generated from the overlap analysis, reviewed with Payroll |
| 2 | Tool A — .NET 8 CLI runner, journal-compatible, your 157 scripts renamed and baselined |
| 3 | Tool B linter + the `SHARED-CHANGE` annotation, wired into CI both sides |
| 4 | Drift snapshots + nightly report; cross-repo impact report |

Phases 0–2 are roughly two days and get your side tracked without needing anything from Payroll. Phase 3 is the first one that needs their buy-in.

---

Want me to start with Phase 0 and the Phase 1 manifest? The manifest draft is the highest-value artifact — it's the thing you'd put in front of the Payroll team to agree the boundary, and I can generate it from the actual script analysis rather than guesswork. I'd produce it as a reviewable table with my ownership guess and the evidence (which scripts in which repo write each table) so you can correct it quickly.
